Do not fire Jensen Huang.

There is no clear replacement for Jensen Huang. We are confi…

The late 1990’s internet analog would suggest that the AI boom is ending, but as I always caveat, price analogs are for “entertainment purposes” only. Then why show them at all, you might ask? Because looking at historical periods of similar price action can be an important conversation starter for how things might be the same or different this time. I use them as loose roadmaps, knowing that at some point the market may travel in a different direction. 

I had failed to realize this before last week, but the inflection point in the 1998-2002 analog was always going to be the midterm election. That could have been a hint that a regime change was in store.

Our message to Nvidia's board:

Do not fire Jensen Huang.

There is no clear replacement for Jensen Huang. We are confident that his departure would ultimately be a net negative for Nvidia, its shareholders, and the AI Revolution.

First, take a look at the data. History also suggests that removing a successful CEO will come with a significant cost.

A study of 187 forced CEO departures from S&P 1500 companies found that removing outperforming CEOs resulted in negative long-term stock returns. This case would be no different, in our view.

Jensen Huang is the definition of an outperforming CEO. Nvidia's board must not make a decision in the heat of the moment.

The board should take the time to conduct a thorough investigation and consult with shareholders, with a strong emphasis on the latter.

Quite literally, Nvidia's board should convene a special shareholder meeting and hold an advisory vote on this decision. This is the most consequential CEO controversy in world history. Shareholders deserve a say.

In addition, Nvidia's stock, $NVDA, is now down -35% in 26 trading days, nearly half of which is a result of the recent scandal.

We believe Jensen Huang's potential removal as CEO is now ~80% priced in.

Why take an action with massive downside potential when the market has already priced in much of that risk?

The downside of retaining Huang may be limited, while the potential upside is tremendous.

Lastly, history shows that retaining Jensen Huang could still lead to a favorable outcome. In 2019, Amazon retained Jeff Bezos as CEO after his extramarital affair became public, and the company's stock subsequently surged +108% by 2021.

Personal misconduct should not be ignored, but it must also be distinguished from corporate wrongdoing and weighed against the consequences of removing an executive who is instrumental to the company's success.

We believe Jensen Huang is an irreplaceable part of Nvidia and the AI Revolution more broadly.

Once the dust settles, firing Jensen Huang would prove to be a costly mistake.

It is time to pause and consult your shareholders.

US pension funds are heavily concentrated in technology stocks:

The technology sector accounts for 44% of total US pension fund equity allocation, according to a Bloomberg analysis of more than 70 pension funds.

This percentage has more than doubled since 2015.

Pension fund equity allocation to technology is now larger than that of the next 3 sectors combined.

By comparison, Financials represent 16%, followed by Healthcare at 12%, Industrials at 11%, and Consumer stocks at 10%.

To put this into perspective, the Consumer sector was these funds' largest allocation in 2014, at ~20%.

US pension funds are more exposed to technology stocks than ever.

Cost effectiveness of AI is becoming a hot topic.

As AI adoption accelerates, the focus is increasingly shifting from simply building more powerful models to maximizing the value generated by every dollar spent.

Not every task requires the most expensive or advanced AI model.

In fact, the global AI inference software market is projected to grow from $21.1 billion in 2026 to $80.9 billion by 2033, representing +283% growth.

As companies deploy AI at scale, reducing costs without sacrificing performance will be increasingly important.

The next phase of AI is about efficiency, not just computing power.

This also marks the 3rd-highest reading on record, surpassed only by the initial pandemic surge in March and April 2020.

Since January 2025, this metric has risen +11.3 percentage points.

Among age groups, consumers under 40 are the most pessimistic, with the perceived probability of higher unemployment at 48.9%, the 2nd-highest reading on record.

By income, this figure among those earning over $100,000 rose to 51.5%, the 2nd-highest reading on record, surpassed only by the 53.9% recorded in March 2020.

Americans are worried about their jobs.

Another look at where the market stands technically is to consider where we are relative to the prevailing trendline. The S&P 500 is in both a cyclical and secular bull market, and while we remain well above the secular trendline, the index is now 5% below the cyclical trendline. That’s less than the previous two lows, set earlier this year at -9% and in 2025 at -14%, so again this suggests that the market has more consolidating/correcting to do.

Note: none of these breakouts are identified in hindsight. Each and every one of them were first discussed as potential setups and once confirmed were tracked and recorded. 

They involve certain amount of subjectivity (my pattern recognition) and selectivity (there can be so many other setups meeting criteria but not considered due to limitations on how many opportunities can be featured).

Berkshire Hathaway is making a historic comeback:

Berkshire Hathaway outperformed the S&P 500 by +19.2 percentage points over the 1 month ending Thursday, its largest rolling monthly outperformance since 2010.

This also ranks as the 4th-largest such outperformance in 30 years.

By comparison, its biggest monthly rolling outperformance occurred during the 2008 Financial Crisis, at +29.6 percentage points.

As of Tuesday's close, the performance gap narrowed to +16.9 percentage points, but it still ranked as one of the largest since 1996.

This comes as Berkshire Hathaway's Class B stock has surged +13.2% over the last month, to an all-time high, while the S&P 500 has declined -3.7% over the same period.

To put this into perspective, Berkshire was underperforming the S&P 500 by -14.3 percentage points in May 2026.

Berkshire Hathaway appears strong, even without Warren Buffett as CEO.
